surfaces.part: wooden frame and stair opening (whole plate)
descending steps inside the frame (step edge lines at rows 17 and 22, risers below them)

answer.evidence: The object is a flat floor plate: a wooden frame of nearly constant width (30 px, rows 1-27) runs along the top and both sides. A dark pit with stacked grey step bands sits inside it. The frame has no front wall and no raised south face. The steps show only short riser bands (rows 18-20, 23-28) under light edge lines at rows 17 and 22, which suggest depth inside the hole, not a standing volume. The silhouette stays rectangular, with no ellipse and no eave or roof. This is a stair-down decal seen from above, which suits the flat kind.

styleAnswer.evidence: The candidate is not a 4x3 ground patch. It is a small stair-down object: a brown wooden frame with grey steps, set on a flat dark grey background. It is much smaller than the grass and paving references and does not read as a ground surface. The measured 8 visible tones per tile is close to paving (7) and above grass (3), but that comes from the frame and steps, not from ground texture. Near-flat coverage is 4%, though the dark grey backdrop and the step faces look like flat fills to the eye. Shading is about 4 steps against roughly 5 in the references. The measured outline is 100% near-neutral dark edge pixels, while the frame shows brown tints, so the outline is mixed. The references show per-stone shading and grass tufts, and the candidate has neither. The kind mismatch means a fair ground-style comparison is not possible, and when in doubt the piece fails.

answer.evidence: This is a stairwell going down, framed in wood. Stacked steps show light front-edge lines at rows 17 and 22. Each is preceded by a tread band (rows 13-16 and 18-21) with a darker shadow row at 21. Below row 22 is a 6-row front face (rows 23-28). The steps are drawn as treads with risers, not as a single flat plate. The kind is flat, but the stairs are rendered with depth. The frame sides are plain vertical strips with no receding side face.

styleAnswer.evidence: The candidate is a small stair-down prop (a wooden frame around steps) on a flat dark grey backdrop. It is not a 4x3 ground patch like the grass and paving references, so the kind does not match. The visible-tone count of 8 per tile is above the grass (3) and the paving (7), but that count is mostly the backdrop, frame and step blocks, not a ground ramp. The dark edge pixels are 100% near-neutral, so the outline reads as a neutral black/grey line, not a dark tone of the adjacent material (the paving reference is 80% neutral, the grass 0%). The main ramps, stone steps and wood frame, show only about 3 lightness steps against roughly 5-6 in the references. Texture is sparse: there is no per-stone shading or grain like the paving's stone-by-stone work. Near-flat coverage is 4%, but the large dark grey backdrop is essentially flat. A careful artist would not accept it beside the references as ground, and it looks flatter and more sticker-like.

surfaces.part: wooden frame, top beam and side posts
dark stairwell opening with descending steps, whole interior

answer.evidence: The object is a 30px-wide framed rectangle: an orange wooden border on rows 1-3 and the side columns, with a dark stairwell interior (rows 4-29). Inside, grey steps are stacked from darkest at the top (rows 5-12) to lighter at the bottom. Each step has a light edge line (rows 17, 22, 28) over a short face (rows 18-20, 23-27). These read as stair treads descending into a pit, seen from above, not as a standing volume. The whole thing is one flat plate inset in the floor with no free-standing south face. That fits the 'flat' kind, so I read it as a top-down slab, not a standing three-quarter object.

styleAnswer.evidence: The candidate is not a 4x3 ground patch. It is a single framed stairwell prop (wood frame, steps, a small item) sitting on a plain dark grey backdrop. The references are continuous surfaces (grass, cobble paving). The measured 8 visible tones per tile beat the references (3 and 7), and near-flat coverage is only 4%, so raw density is not the problem. But 100% of the dark edge pixels are neutral, which matches the near-black 'sticker' outline. The frame and steps show about 3-4 lightness steps against Beodeul's 5-6 per material. By eye, the wood and stone have little per-element grain or highlights compared with the individually shaded cobbles in the paving reference. The backdrop is a dull, uniform fill with no ground texture. Because the kind does not match and the outline is neutral and shallow, it fails.

surfaces.part: lower step, edge and front face

answer.evidence: This is a staircase going down, seen from the south inside a wooden frame. The upper step has a tread band at rows 13-16 that ends in a lighter edge line at row 17 (L=114 against 83). Below it is a front face at rows 18-20 and a darker shadow row at 21. The lower step has a bright edge line at row 22 (L=155) above a front face at rows 23-28. The frame sides and dark back wall are vertical or recessed and show no isometric side face. The lower step has no separate tread above its edge line, so the top surfaces are thin and ambiguous. The tread at rows 13-16 with an edge line and a front face below is still enough to read as three-quarter, though weakly. The kind 'flat' fits loosely, since a stair-down opening is a floor feature.
